title: C Program Structure
description: The anatomy of a C program: #include, main(), statements, braces, semicolons, comments, and identifiers.
objectives: Understand the required structure of a runnable C program
Follow C naming and commenting conventions

content.heading: #include and main()
content.body: Every C program needs an int main() function — the entry point the operating system's loader calls first when the program runs. #include <header.h> directives (angle brackets for standard library headers, double quotes "header.h" for your own project headers) pull in declarations needed for the functions you use — #include <stdio.h> is needed for printf/scanf, for instance. main() conventionally returns an int, by convention 0 for success and a non-zero value to signal an error to the calling shell/process, accessible via the exit code.

content.heading: Statements, Blocks, Comments, and Identifiers
content.body: Every statement ends with a semicolon. Curly braces {} group statements into a block, defining the body of a function, loop, or conditional (mandatory for a function body; optional, but recommended, for single-statement loop/if bodies). Comments come in two forms: // single-line (from C99 onward) and /* multi-line */ (available since the original C standard). Identifiers (variable, function, type names) follow the same general rule as most C-family languages: letters, digits, and underscores, not starting with a digit, case-sensitive, and not a reserved keyword (int, if, for, return, and about 30 others).

content.explanation: The #include brings in printf's declaration. main() returns 0, the conventional success exit code read by the shell or calling process.

keyPoints: int main() is the required entry point of a standard C program
#include <stdio.h> (angle brackets) for standard headers; #include "file.h" (quotes) for your own
Every statement ends with a semicolon; braces {} delimit blocks
main() returning 0 conventionally signals success to the operating system
commonMistakes: Forgetting to #include a header needed for a function like printf() or malloc()
Missing a semicolon at the end of a statement
Confusing angle-bracket includes (<...>) with quoted includes ("...") and their different search paths
